newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Woman flees N.Korea across tense border to South.
newsitem.headline: Woman flees N.Korea across tense border to South.

text.p: A woman fled impoverished North Korea on Thursday across the heavily-fortified border with South Korea, as Seoul held talks in Beijing aimed at allowing a senior Pyongyang official sheltering in its mission there to come to the South.
The Defence Ministry said the woman in her 20s defected to the South at about 10:20 a.m. (0120 GMT) through the eastern sector of the demilitarised zone (DMZ) bisecting the Korean peninsula.
A terse ministry statement did not say how she had managed to elude heavy concentrations of communist troops guarding one of the world's tensest frontiers.

The four-km (2.5 mile) wide DMZ was created as a buffer zone between the rival states under the 1953 truce agreement which ended the Korean War, but the zone, sealed off from the public by barbed wire, has since been sown with thousands of mines. Both sides have installed many advanced weapons there.
The young woman's motives for fleeing were being investigated, the statement said.
Her defection coincided with the funeral of another defector who was shot earlier this month by two suspected North Korean gunmen just south of Seoul.

Diplomats said the latest defection could complicate talks between Seoul and Beijing over the fate of Hwang Jang-yop, holed up at Seoul's consular office in the Chinese capital since arriving there with an aide on Febuary 12 and seeking asylum.

The talks about Hwang, the most senior official to flee North Korea, resumed on Wednesday after being suspended following the death last week of Chinese leader Deng Xiaoping. South Korean officials have so far reported no progress.

Hwang's defection placed further strain on relations between the two Koreas, which had just begun to reopen contacts frozen after a North Korean submarine dropped 26 intruders on a Southern beach last September.

Three days after Hwang sought asylum in Beijing, North Korean defector Li Il-nam was shot in the head at the doorway to a friend's apartment where he had been staying. Li, known in South Korea as Lee Han-yong, died on Tuesday.
South Korean police said on Thursday that Li's friend had received a letter threatening him and his wife for cooperating with police probing the shooting.
"The letter said the couple would face retaliation if they cooperated with our investigation and their apartment would be blown up," police spokesman Ha Seung-gyun said by telephone.
Police are working on the theory that Pyongyang instructed its agents to murder Li as a warning to South Korea and other North Korean escapees following Hwang's defection.
South Korean police have virtually ruled out earlier suspicions that Lee might have been gunned down by loan sharks or underworld hitmen, police spokesman Ha Seung-gyun said.

Li, who was the nephew of Pyongyang leader Kim Jong-il's ex-wife, ran into financial trouble after he defected to the South in 1982 and went into business. He spent 10 months in jail in 1993 for embezzling funds.
There was no immediate response from North Korea over Thursday's defection.

A South Korean Foreign Ministry official said it was possible there would be no early conclusion to the Seoul-Beijing talks over Hwang as Chinese authorities were anxious not to offend Pyongyang. Hwang's defection faced Beijing with a difficult choice over whether to offend its old communist ally or its new capitalist friend.
Analysts say, however, that China will in the end almost certainly allow Hwang, the architect of North Korea's governing ideology of fanatic self-reliance, to go to Seoul.
